blocks.x: . This is the same machine we had before. We can't buy a new one. Can I get your name down again?
You want to start it with my name?
Oh yes, give me your name. The Redder Roller 11.
You should have put that roll on. Roller is my favorite grandson, but he don't love them all. He's doing too swell to worry about his grandma now. She's the one that inspired him all the way through.
And let's see, the day is... June 1st. June 1st, 1967. And where are we?
We're at 3143 Tipper Mall. We don't put Irish Channel because it's not. I wrote a piece with a French Quarter paper about the expressway and they put Irish Channel on it.
But you don't consider this Irish Channel? No, I don't. Where is Irish Channel?
Irish Channel is down to where the project is. Or the St. Thomas Project there? Yeah, around that way. I used to live there. If it was Irish Channel, there were some mighty nice people living there.
But did you live in this neighborhood all your lives? No, I haven't. Where all have you lived?
I lived all over the city.
All over the city?
I never did live in Newport and Louisiana Avenue to Felicity Street.
From Louisiana to Felicity? Yeah. And from Chippewa, how far back?
That's all. Where's back? I lived in Louisiana in 1928. My aunt, she died and I came here. Pretty much all the other across the street.
How far back towards the lake did you get? Never did. Always along Chippewa Street.

Mr. Golda lived back. They're too quiet for me. I like it. They got a ball in the corner and they hear all the music and the jazz every night. I don't know why I never went. I walked to the center and hear the music.
Did you ever live on Magazine Street? Constance?

No, I lived on Sixth and Conn. Sixth and Conn. I enrolled in the Dallas State about two years. That's when I left Birmingham. Actually lost a little girl. And they lived there two years. Johnny took a demotion and came back. That's why I lost her baby in Birmingham. She wasn't going to say that. The little girl that she was around. She wasn't blind. I had to go there for six weeks. Doctor said she could never have any more children.
Did you ever live on the other side of Magazine Street? No. Well, you were going to tell me some things about jazz. You had some more thoughts? Do you remember some things? Yeah, I got it here.
I'm going to read it. I got to talk in the name. You got it on now? Yeah, it's on. Oh. Well, I was going to talk about the band at Badu. Do you want some paper? Yeah. Okay, go ahead.
Stop.

The average band in 1917 had five men. By 1925 it was eight or ten. But until 1930 a twelve man set up was considered unusual. The 1920s was the golden age of the small bands, whether they were good jazz bands or bad society bands.
After a while the small bands declined.

Every town and village had its own orchestra. When you attended a movie or a Broadway show, bands played in the pits. As it was called, another stage built in from the picture screen. Instead, such gage could be lowered to any level, but a band would play there. I remember Lewis Prima at the Sangers in said band. That's how he became famous. He surely could play like trumpet and jazz. I stayed for two shows and I went every week just to hear him play. And he really played jazz and he is still playing. 1926 was the end of Waterville. We was on stage at all the shows, Tulane and Crescent. They were the high class shows, then at Mission High. Sound music, sound movies there beginning, put an end to the small bands. No orchestra. This was between 1926 to 1938. Sound movies came into 1928 when they had the sound movies. And then they put bands on the stage. Of course at this time, the radio at 1926, we had a phonograph.
